fixes.explanation: Right, baker. Daniel 3:5 says that when they hear the music, they "…must fall down and worship the golden statue…" the king set up. The music was the cue, and the cue was a full band. The list runs from the horn and flute all the way to the pipes and all kinds of music.

Furnace, baker. Daniel 3:6 says whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. The herald proclaimed it loudly, too. I know a thing or two about hot ovens, and I would not want to stand near that one.

True, baker. Daniel 3:7 says that as soon as they heard the music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue. Everyone went down on cue, every nation and every language. I bet that was something to see, a whole crowd going down at once.

Seven, baker. Daniel 3:19 says he gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual. It was Nebuchadnezzar who gave that order. I burn a batch at the regular heat and I'm still sorry about it for days.

False, baker. Daniel 3:27 says the fire had no effect on their bodies, and there was no smell of fire on them. Not a hair of their heads was singed, either. They came out of a furnace seven times hotter than usual and didn't smell like it.

True, baker. In Daniel 3:29 the king decrees that anyone of any nation or language who says anything offensive against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be cut into pieces. The decree also says their houses would be reduced to rubble. It's a harsh decree, and it's what the text says.

Promoted, baker. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon. It's the same province they were already managing. They went from the furnace to a better job.
Silver is a fine metal, but it isn't what the text says. Daniel 3:1 says the king made a golden statue. Gold is the word the verse uses.
Twelve is a lot smaller than what the text says, friend. Daniel 3:1 says sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. Sixty is five times what you picked.

The lions' den is a famous spot in the book of Daniel (Daniel 6:16), so I see why you went there. But that's a different story, and this herald never mentions it. Daniel 3:6 says anyone who doesn't worship will be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace.

Arioch is a name from the book of Daniel (Daniel 2:14), but he isn't in this story. Daniel 3:12 has the astrologers telling the king that these are Jews you have appointed. The one who put them in charge was Nebuchadnezzar.

The herald proclaimed the command, friend, but the astrologers point somewhere else. In Daniel 3:12 they tell the king, "…you have appointed…" these men to manage the province. So the appointing came from King Nebuchadnezzar.
Three is a nice number, since there are three men, but it's not the one. Daniel 3:19 says he gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual. It's seven, friend.

The text doesn't say they ran, friend. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames killed the men who carried Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego up. It's a heavy detail, and it shows how hot that furnace was.
That's not what the king saw, friend. Daniel 3:25 says, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…" Walking around, and four instead of three.
A prophet is a reasonable guess, friend. But Daniel 3:28 has the king say that God "…has sent His angel…" Angel is the word he uses.
A priest isn't who the king names, friend. In Daniel 3:28 the king says God "…has sent His angel and delivered His servants…" It's an angel in his words.
